Artifact Description

For Milestone Four, I improved the database system in my Weight Tracker mobile app. I originally built this app in CS-360, and back then it only used one simple SQLite table to store weight entries. That design worked for the basic version of the app, but it was not flexible enough for the new features I wanted to add in my capstone. So, for this milestone, I redesigned the entire database layer to make it more organized, more secure, and capable of supporting multiple types of data.

Why I Included This Artifact in My ePortfolio

I chose this artifact because the database work I did shows real technical skill and problem-solving ability. Databases are a huge part of computer science, and I wanted to show that I can design and implement a proper relational database instead of relying on a single table. The enhancements I made demonstrate that I understand how to structure data, enforce relationships, and write clean data-access code.

Here are the main improvements I made:

1. Built a Full Relational Database Schema

I replaced the old single-table setup with a relational schema that includes five tables:

Users

Goals

WorkoutHistory

WorkoutEntries

Recommendations

Each table has a primary key, and several of them use foreign keys to link back to the Users table. I also added indexes to speed up queries that filter by user ID. This design is much closer to what real applications use and makes the app easier to expand.

2. Added DAO-Style Methods for Data Access

Instead of writing raw SQL everywhere, I added structured methods like:

getAllWorkoutHistory()

deleteWorkoutHistory(long id)

These methods make the code cleaner and easier to maintain. They also help keep the database logic separate from the UI logic, which is an important part of good software design.

3. Updated Model Classes to Match the Database

I created new model classes such as WorkoutHistory, User, Goal, and others. These classes match the structure of the database tables and make it easier to pass data around the app. I also updated WeightHistoryActivity and WeightAdapter so they use the new WorkoutHistory model instead of the old WeightEntry class.

4. Added Secure Password Hashing

To improve security, I added SHA-256 hashing for user passwords. This means the app never stores plain-text passwords in the database. Even though this is not a full security system, it shows that I understand the importance of protecting user data.

5. Enabled Support for New Features

The new database design supports several features that were not possible before, including:

Multi-user accounts

Step tracking

Workout logs

Goal tracking

Recommendation storage

All of these depend on the relational structure I built.

Testing and Validation

To verify that the redesigned relational database functioned correctly, I performed testing on database relationships, CRUD operations, password hashing, and multi-user functionality. These tests confirmed that data integrity was maintained, users remained isolated from one another, and security controls functioned as expected.

Database Integrity Validation

The database was tested after migrating from the original single-table design to the new five-table relational architecture. Users, goals, workout history records, recommendations, and workout entries were successfully created, updated, retrieved, and deleted without relationship failures or application crashes. DAO methods returned expected results and all foreign key relationships remained intact during testing.

Course Outcomes Demonstrated

This enhancement helped me make progress toward several CS program outcomes:

Software engineering and database design: I designed a normalized schema, added foreign keys, and wrote structured DAO methods.

Security mindset: I implemented password hashing to protect user credentials.

Professional communication: The code is organized and commented, and the narrative explains my decisions clearly.

Algorithmic integration: The database now supports the RecommendationEngine I built in Milestone Three.

I met the outcomes I planned to cover in Module One, and I do not need to update my coverage plan.

Reflection on the Enhancement Process

Redesigning the database taught me a lot about how important structure and planning are. Switching from one table to five tables meant I had to update almost every part of the app, including the model classes, activities, and adapter. One of the hardest parts was making sure all the new relationships worked correctly and that the app did not break when I switched to the new WorkoutHistory model.

Another challenge was making sure the DAO methods were efficient and did not cause crashes. I had to evaluate them carefully to make sure the queries returned the right data. Overall, this enhancement helped me understand how real applications manage data and how important it is to design a database that can grow with the app.

The result is a much more professional and scalable database system that supports all the new features I added in earlier milestones. I am confident that this enhancement shows my ability to work with databases in a real-world way, and that’s why it belongs in my ePortfolio.
